title: Area and Volume, Part 3: Traps and the Fast Way

beats.say: In this video, we look at five mistakes students make with area and volume, and then use Desmos to confirm a volume and to find a missing dimension.
Each trap is shown as a wrong line first, then the right line, with the reason it's so tempting.
Trap one. A circle with a diameter of ten has a radius of five. Students put the diameter into the area formula.
Halve the diameter first. The radius is five, and the area is pi times five squared, which is twenty-five pi.
Trap two. The volume of a cone or a pyramid has a factor of one third. Students use the cylinder or prism formula by mistake.
A cone holds one third of the matching cylinder. So the volume is one third times pi r squared times the height.
Trap three. If every edge of a box is doubled, students double the volume.
Volume scales by the cube of the scale factor. Two cubed is eight, so the volume is multiplied by eight. Area is multiplied by four.
Trap four. A cone has a radius of five and a slant height of thirteen. Students use the slant height as the height in the volume formula.
The height is perpendicular to the base. Use the Pythagorean theorem with the radius and the slant height. Thirteen squared minus five squared is one hundred forty-four, so the height is twelve.
Trap five. In a composite figure, a semicircle is only half of a circle. Students use the area of the full circle.
A semicircle has half the area of the full circle. So the area is one half times pi r squared.
Most of these questions are one formula plus careful arithmetic. Write the formula, substitute, and then simplify. Leave pi in until the end, since answers are often written as k pi.
For scaling questions, skip the formulas entirely. Find the length ratio k, then use k squared for area, and k cubed for volume.

card.text: Scaling: k² for area, k³ for volume

beats.say: Desmos helps with arithmetic that involves pi. To confirm the cone's volume, type one third times pi times four squared times twenty-seven, and compare the result with one hundred forty-four pi.
Open a fresh graph. We'll type the cone's volume in one line.
Type one, a slash, and three. Press the right arrow to leave the fraction, then type times pi times four squared, and press the right arrow, then times twenty-seven.
Desmos shows about four hundred fifty-two point four. And one hundred forty-four times pi is also about four hundred fifty-two point four, so they match.
Desmos can also find a missing dimension. A sphere has a volume of two hundred eighty-eight pi. To find its radius, graph the volume formula and the value, and find where they meet.
We type the volume of a sphere as a function of the radius x, and a horizontal line at the given volume.
Type y equals four thirds times pi times x cubed. Remember the right arrows after the fraction and after the exponent.
Now type y equals two hundred eighty-eight times pi. This horizontal line is the given volume.
Click the crossing point. The x value is six. So the sphere's radius is six.
Now a practice problem. A cone has a radius of three and a height of twelve. Find its volume in terms of pi. Pause the video, try it, and then watch the solution.

card.sub: Find the volume. Pause and try it first.

beats.say: Use the cone formula, one third pi r squared h, with a radius of three and a height of twelve.
Three squared is nine. So the volume is one third times pi times nine times twelve.
Nine times twelve is one hundred eight, and one third of one hundred eight is thirty-six. So the volume is thirty-six pi.
To recap. Use the radius, not the diameter. Remember the one third for cones, and use the perpendicular height.
Scale volume by k cubed and area by k squared, and use half a circle for a semicircle.
beats.item: k³ for volume, k² for area; half a circle

beats.say: Use Desmos for arithmetic with pi, or to solve for a missing dimension. In the next topic, we study lines, angles, and triangles.
